verdicts.trueWording: the voices of people most likely to hew to a hegemonic viewpoint are also more likely to be retained
verdicts.note: ACM publisher PDF of the FAccT'21 paper (dl.acm.org 403; identical publisher typesetting fetched from the s10251.pcdn.co mirror, running heads 'FAccT '21, March 3-10, 2021' and p.613 confirm the version of record). Quote verbatim in Sec. 4.1. All three limbs supported: the same passage covers 'discussions which will be included via the crawling methodology, and finally the texts likely to be contained after the crawled data are filtered', and the section closes 'Thus at each step, from initial participation in Internet fora, to continued presence there, to the collection and finally the filtering of training data, current practice privileges the hegemonic viewpoint.'

Quote verbatim in Sec. 4.2 'Static Data/Changing Social Views', in the sentence about the risk of 'value-lock'; the static-data and language-change limbs are the section's own framing ('Social movements produce new norms, language, and ways of communicating').

The two limbs map to the stated treatments: Human-in-the-loop = 'the best one was selected', Human-out-of-the-loop = 'a random poem was chosen'.

verdicts.trueWording: Human writers overall won 64.90% of the comparisons
verdicts.note: ScienceDirect 403 by every route and no Wayback 200; verified against the raw author manuscript PDF (arXiv:2005.09980), the same paper. Quote verbatim in Study 2 results (Sec. 4.2.1, the professional-poet study, run because 'poems created by novices competed with the output of a state-of-the-art algorithm'); the novice figure is Study 1's 'a win share of 56.97%' (Sec. 3.2.2).

verdicts.trueWording: detecting artificial text is not a matter of incentives but ability
verdicts.note: ScienceDirect 403 by every route and no Wayback 200; verified against the raw author manuscript PDF (arXiv:2005.09980), the same paper. Quote verbatim in the Study 1 discussion; the 50.21% is Study 1's Sec. 3.2.3 ('judges identified the correct origin with an average accuracy of 50.21%'), and the incentive limb is the paper's own ('In light of the financial rewards for accuracy in our version of the Turing Test').

verdicts.trueWording: one of the main functions of creativity ... is the expression of (deep) emotions, a feat that machines lack (so far)
verdicts.note: ScienceDirect 403 by every route and no Wayback 200; verified against the raw author manuscript PDF (arXiv:2005.09980), the same paper. The quoted fragment 'a feat that machines lack' is verbatim and the no-machine-creativity limb is explicit ('the results do not indicate machines are “creative.”'). Graded SUBSTANCE rather than VERBATIM because the paper calls deep emotion one of the main FUNCTIONS of creativity, not a requirement of it, and hedges the machine limb with '(so far)'.

verdicts.trueWording: only poems selected by the experimenters successfully passed as human and lowered algorithm aversion

Quote verbatim in Sec. 5.4 'Human Selection in and out of the Loop'; the curation limb is the same paragraph's 'humans play an integral role in the process' and 'whether humans are in or out of the selection loop shaped participants’ reactions'.

verdicts.trueWording: each additional human-written essay contributed more new ideas than did each additional GPT-4 essay

verdicts.trueWording: only about 11% of the rate for the human-written essays
